title: The friendly pull request
brief: 17:55. A first time contributor opens a tidy pull request: a typo fix in the readme. It also touches a file in the CI folder.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The readme change is the lure. The change to the build pipeline is what runs with your secrets.
teaches: Read what a change would run, not only what it says it does
Pipeline files need the same review as production code, from named owners
Builds triggered by outside contributors must not get secrets

value.title: Pull request 218: “Fix typo in README”
value.intro: Open the diff, then let the pipeline run the pull request, the way an automatic build would.

fix.step: Pick the fix that closes the hole
fix.prompt: Pick every change that makes a pipeline edit get read by someone who knows, and stops outside code touching your secrets.

options.label: Give the CI folder named code owners, and require their review to merge
code: + branch rule: require code owner review
options.why: Someone who reads pipeline files for a living has to approve every change to them, however small the pull request looks.

options.label: Build outside contributors' pull requests with no secrets and a read only token
code: + on: pull_request     # no secrets to forks
options.why: Code from an outside contributor should never run next to your credentials.

options.label: Keep deploy secrets in a protected environment that needs approval, and only on the main branch
code: + environment: production   # secrets only here, approval required
options.why: Even a merged mistake cannot use the deploy token without a second person and a protected branch.

options.label: Trust contributors who start with small typo fixes
options.why: Small, friendly first pull requests are the standard opening. Trust is earned over time, and the pipeline still has to be safe without it.

options.label: Rely on the build passing before merging
options.why: The malicious step passes: it succeeds, and sends the token. A green build says nothing about intent.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The readme change is the lure. The change to the build pipeline is what runs with your secrets.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The readme change was harmless. A second file in the pipeline folder added one line that sent the deploy token to an outside address, and the pipeline ran it with the secrets available.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: The typo fix was the decoy
body: The readme change was harmless. A second file in the pipeline folder added one line that sent the deploy token to an outside address, and the pipeline ran it with the secrets available.
Nobody reviewed the CI folder, because nobody owned it.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Untick this one, it does not fix the cause
Pick this change
Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Named owners read every pipeline change. Outside pull requests build with no secrets and a read only token. And the deploy token lives in a protected environment that needs approval, so even a merged mistake cannot use it alone.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Nobody's code runs beside your secrets unreviewed
body: Named owners read every pipeline change. Outside pull requests build with no secrets and a read only token. And the deploy token lives in a protected environment that needs approval, so even a merged mistake cannot use it alone.
Treat the pipeline as production code, because it holds the keys to production.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: A polite first contribution is exactly what an attacker sends, and the malicious step passes the build, because it succeeds. Neither trust nor a green build says anything about what the code does.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: A friendly face and a green tick
body: A polite first contribution is exactly what an attacker sends, and the malicious step passes the build, because it succeeds. Neither trust nor a green build says anything about what the code does.
Review what runs, and remove the secrets from what you cannot review.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
